newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia ministers say Lee's court move positive.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia ministers say Lee's court move positive.

text.p: Malaysian ministers were reported on Tuesday to view as positive Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew's decision to ask a court to delete from the record his criticism of a Malaysian state.
"This statement is certainly more positive than his earlier statement," Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was quoted as saying by New Straits Times daily.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said Lee's attempt was positive in resolving the diplomatic row, the newspaper said. "It's a good development," Abdullah was quoted as saying.

Lee, former Singapore prime minister who now holds the portfolio of Senior Minister, said he would ask the Singapore court to delete his statement in an affidavit that the Malaysian state of Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
The remark about Johor, which is just across the causeway from Singapore, incensed Kuala Lumpur.

"Malaysian government leaders have expressed their wish that statements in my affidavit which have caused offence to the Malaysian people not remain on the record," Lee said in a signed statement on Monday.
"My counsel will apply to court for permission to delete the offending statements so that they will no longer remain on the record," he said.
Both Anwar and Abdullah said the latest move would be taken into account at the Malaysian cabinet's weekly meeting on Wednesday, when the issue is down for discussion.
Before Lee issued Monday's statement, Malaysia had said the cabinet would discuss whether to take any further action in view of its demands for a full retraction.
Last week, Lee apologised unreservedly for the remarks, which were made as part of a libel action against an opposition politician and which he had not expected to become public.
In Monday's statement, Lee repeated that apology.

His controversial remarks were in an affidavit on January 27 in proceedings against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong, who fled to Johor Baru, capital of Johor state, immediately after losing a race for parliament in Singapore's general elections on January 2.
Tang had said he feared for his life in Singapore because he had received death threats. Lee questioned why he would feel safer in Johor.
